An aquarium’s filter does far more than keep the water looking clean. It continuously removes waste, circulates oxygen, and provides a home for beneficial bacteria that break down harmful toxins produced by fish and uneaten food. Without proper filtration, ammonia and other toxic compounds can quickly build up, turning a healthy aquarium into a dangerous environment for its inhabitants. A good filtration system helps maintain water quality, stabilize the ecosystem, and keep fish healthy over the long term. While decorations and lighting may catch the eye, the filter is the unseen engine that keeps the entire aquarium alive.

Cleaning a fish tank doesn't always mean draining it. In this method, waste and debris are removed while the water stays in place. Tools like siphon vacuums and filtration systems pull out uneaten food, algae, and sediment from the gravel, keeping the environment clean without stressing the fish. What makes this approach effective is balance. Beneficial bacteria remain undisturbed, water chemistry stays stable, and the tank continues to cycle naturally. It's a low-impact way to maintain a healthy aquarium, showing how smart maintenance can work with the ecosystem instead of resetting it. This video is for educational purposes only. I often get asked how I keep my water clear, especially when it comes to taking videos on my phone. I think one of the biggest factors in getting good aquarium videos is simply having clear water! Obviously, make sure your glass is clean and free of water spots, but beyond that, a lot of it comes down to water clarity. For me, plants and microorganisms definitely do a lot of the heavy lifting. Compared to my Walstad tank, though, I’d say this tank is just a little bit clearer, and I think that’s thanks in part to the sponge filter. I know everyone has their own opinions about filtration and what works best for their tanks, but personally, I’m a big fan of sponge filters. Here’s why: 🌿 Gentle, adjustable flow: I actually use a little control valve to adjust the airflow. During the day, when I have my DIY CO2 running, I turn it down for a gentler flow. At night, when the CO2 is off, I’ll often turn it up a bit to encourage more water movement throughout the tank. I noticed that when I increase the flow overnight, there’s noticeably less debris sitting on the bottom of the tank the following morning! 🦠 Great surface area for beneficial bacteria: The sponge provides plenty of surface area for beneficial bacteria to colonize, supporting biological filtration. 💧 Low maintenance: I really only rinse mine in tank water when I notice debris, leaves, or other plant matter accumulating on it. This is usually once every month or two, depending on how much I’ve been trimming and moving things around in the tank. 🦐 Safe for small inhabitants: No worrying about tiny shrimp or fry getting sucked into the filter! 🔬 A little hangout for microorganisms: The sponge also creates a great place for little organisms to gather. My gobies will often hang around this filter because they know there’s a pretty good supply of scuds, copepods, and ostracods living in and around it. And finally, I love how easy they are to hide! The video here is actually showing the back of my tank. From the front, you can barely see the filter itself, aside from the airline tubing. One other reason I particularly love this Hygger sponge filter is that it also has ceramic pearls in the bottom, which provide additional surface area for beneficial bacteria and another layer of biological filtration compared to an ordinary sponge filter. Since switching to this one, I can honestly say my water has been pretty clear! Obviously, every aquarium is different, and there’s no single filtration method that works for everyone. But for my planted tanks, sponge filters have been a great fit! 🌱 #Aquascaping #PlantedTank #spongefilter #clearwater #aquaticplants
